content.text:
Found two related problems and fixed all three touch points.

**Root cause (most cards):** When a card subscene has no choices left, Dendry shows a default “Continue…” button that goes to `rootSceneId`. That defaults to the `root` scene (start menu / setup), not `main`. Cards like contracting, community outreach, etc. hit this on their leaf subscenes.

**Explicit wrong targets:**
- `shuffle_cabinet` — “No, there is no need.” used `@root`
- `cancel_advisor_action` — had `go-to: root`

**Fixes:**

1. **`main.scene.dry`** — added `set-root: ok` so once you reach the main hand, “Continue…” on card subscenes returns to `main` instead of the start menu.

2. **`cancel_advisor_action.scene.dry`** — changed `go-to: root` → `go-to: main`.

3. **`shuffle_cabinet.scene.dry`** — changed `@root` → `@return` for the decline option.

Build and lint both pass. After reloading, finishing a card action should return you to the main hand; shuffle cabinet decline and advisor cancel should as well. Existing saves will pick up the new `rootSceneId` the next time they visit `main`.

content.text:
Two changes work together: **`@return` on card menus** and **hand restoration in `return.scene.dry`**.

### Why this was needed
Playing a card removes it from your hand (`playCard`). Most deck cards had no way to back out — only a default “Continue…” after committing to an action. Advisors already used `- @return`; regular cards did not.

### `return.scene.dry`
When you `@return` from a played card, it now puts that card back in the main hand (if there’s room), using the previous scene to find the card root. Pinned advisor cards are unchanged — they never leave the pinned row.

### Cards updated with `- @return`
Added on the **top-level menu** of every deck card:

- community_outreach, contracting, activist_training, coop_economy, education, magic, migrations, peer_media  
- militia_degrade, municipal_ai, security  

`shuffle_cabinet` already had `@return` (“No, there is no need.”).

**Contracting submenus** also got `@return` so you can back out mid-choice:

- `@big_3`, `@local_wealthy`, `@cooperatives`

### Intentional omission on leaf choices
Subscenes where an action already fires on entry (e.g. “Calm the first wave settlers”) still end with “Continue…” only — the effect is already applied, so putting the card back in hand wouldn’t make sense.

Rebuild is done; reload and you should see a return option on card menus that puts the card back in your hand if you haven’t taken an action yet.

content.text:
Created `scripts/optimize-prosperity-balance.js` and wired it as `npm run optimize-prosperity`.

### Script behavior

Each evaluation:
1. Bootstraps election + economic runtimes from `.dry` scenes (same as `simulate-prosperity-months.js`)
2. Seeds starter assets and applies linkage coefficients from the parameter vector
3. Snapshots population-weighted block prosperity **after** seeding, **before** simulation
4. Runs **6 months** of prosperity tick (asset prosperity → connection bleed → housing)
5. Computes loss:

```
loss = residualMult × Σ pop×(final−initial)² / Σ pop  +  linkWeight × Σ|linkage coeffs|
```

**Tuned parameters (68 total):**
- 11 starter asset batch counts (`STARTER_ECONOMIC_ASSET_BATCHES`)
- 57 non-zero linkage coefficients (intra-district mesh + IG→home-district strata links)

**Fixed (not tuned):** affluence self-decay rows, Docks trade spill, Pitts crime, housing flow.

**CLI:**
```bash
npm run optimize-prosperity -- --iterations 300 --residual-mult 50 --link-weight 1 --verbose
npm run optimize-prosperity -- --show-decays
npm run optimize-prosperity -- --json-out out/prosperity-optim-result.json
```

`--residual-mult` is the prosperity-stability knob you asked for. Raise it to prioritize staying near initial prosperity over keeping links small.

Also fixed a bad path in `simulate-prosperity-months.js` (`cards/local_organizing/...`).

---

### Affluence self-decay table (sanity check)

From `Q.prosperityConnectionCatalog` in `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`.  
Formula: `monthly Δ ≈ coefficient × prosperity` (`basis=level`, `self_feedback=true`).

| ID | Scope | Target | Coefficient | Δ @ prosperity 6 | Δ @ prosperity 10 |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| decay_rich | stratum | rich | −0.05 | −0.300 | −0.500 |
| decay_first | stratum | first | −0.05 | −0.300 | −0.500 |
| decay_second | stratum | second | −0.105 | −0.630 | −1.050 |
| decay_coop | stratum | coop | −0.25 | −1.500 | −2.500 |
| decay_drone | stratum | drone | −0.02 | −0.120 | −0.200 |
| decay_alien | stratum | alien | −0.02 | −0.120 | −0.200 |
| decay_deeper | stratum | deeper | −0.02 | −0.120 | −0.200 |
| decay_third_wave | stratum | third_wave | −0.05 | −0.300 | −0.500 |

**Notes:**
- Stratum rows affect every voter block of that stratum (all districts).
- Big Three IGs decay **15× faster** than syndicates at the same prosperity index.

- A smoke test on baseline params gave loss ≈ **35.6** after 6 months (assets push prosperity up faster than decays/mesh pull it down).

content.text:
The broken links came from a **Dendry parse error** in `@terms_menu`, not from the tax options themselves.

The hub had section headings (`= Security & jurisdiction`, `= Courts & rights`, etc.) **between** groups of `- @` choices. Dendry requires all choices in one contiguous block — any prose or headings after the first choice makes the whole scene fail to compile. That meant `cable_break_negotiations` never made it into the build, so every link to it (terms menu, corporate tax, dev jump, cable break event) was dead.

**Fix:** Removed the interleaved section headings and flattened `@terms_menu` into a single choice list. Also changed inline `@police_funding` in disband prose to plain text so it doesn’t render as a broken link.

`npm run make-html` succeeds now, so all negotiation options should work again. If you want the section groupings back visually, we can do it with category sub-menus (e.g. `@terms_security` → police/tax/disband) without breaking the parser.

content.text:
All reprisal knobs now have inline comments naming the demand they belong to. There’s also a **rival schadenfreude** block (`CABLE_NEG_RELIEF_*`) for options where one megacorp enjoys a rival’s setback.

**Rival relief applies on:**
| Demand | Hurt | Relieved (enjoys rival’s pain) |
|--------|------|--------------------------------|
| Vats police | Soylent +2 | Magrail −1 |
| Railyard police | Magrail +2 | Soylent −1 |
| Docks police | Soylent +1, Magrail +1 | Brazos −1 |
| Limelight police | Brazos +3 | Soylent −1, Magrail −1 |
| Tax (half/full, belligerents only) | Soylent & Magrail | Brazos −1 |
| Mixed ceasefire trials | Soylent +1, Magrail +1 | Brazos −1 |

**Rules enforced in code:**
- Relief only runs when gross reprisal raised ≥ **2** on that pick
- Total relief is always **strictly less** than total raised (net reprisal still goes up)
- If knobs would break that, relief is auto-clamped so net gain is at least 1

Withdraw paths mirror the same math, so removing a demand restores rival relief too. Demands that hit everyone equally (payroll, civil rights, infra cap, tax-all-three, etc.) have no relief — edit only the `CABLE_NEG_REPR_*` lines for those.

#!/usr/bin/env node
const fs = require('fs')
const path = require('path')
const file = path.join(__dirname, '../source/scenes/major/cable_break_negotiations.scene.dry')
let text = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')

text = text.replace(
  'on-arrival: {!\n// --- reprisal knobs',
  'on-arrival: {!\nQ.cableNegEnsureApi = function() {\n// --- reprisal knobs'
)

text = text.replace(
  /\/\/ --- bootstrap \(sketch: wire vote tally \+ budget costs in a later pass\) ---\nif \(Q\.cable_neg_ready != 1\) \{[\s\S]*?Q\.cable_neg_infra_cap = 0\n\}\nfunction cableNegReprisalAdd/,
  `Q.cableNegLeverageBoost = CABLE_NEG_LEVERAGE_BOOST
if (Q._cable_neg_api) return
Q._cable_neg_api = 1
Q.cableNegReprisalAdd = function`
)

text = text.replace(/^function (cableNeg\w+)\(/gm, 'Q.$1 = function(')

const syncMarker = 'Q.cableNegSyncCorpStances = function()'
const syncIdx = text.indexOf(syncMarker)
const apiStart = text.indexOf('Q.cableNegReprisalAdd = function')
let apiBlock = text.slice(apiStart, syncIdx)
apiBlock = apiBlock.replace(/\bQ\.(cableNeg\w+)/g, '___Q___$1')
apiBlock = apiBlock.replace(/\bcableNeg(\w+)\(/g, 'Q.cableNeg$1(')
apiBlock = apiBlock.replace(/___Q___(cableNeg\w+)/g, 'Q.$1')
text = text.slice(0, apiStart) + apiBlock + text.slice(syncIdx)

text = text.replace(
  /(Q\.cableNegSyncCorpStances = function\(\) \{[\s\S]*?stanceFor\('brazos'\)\n\})\nif \(typeof Q\.syncIgAttitudes/,
  `$1
}
Q.cableNegEnsureApi()
if (Q.cable_neg_ready != 1) {
    Q.cable_neg_ready = 1
    Q.cable_neg_leverage_boost = Q.cableNegLeverageBoost

    Q.brazos_leverage = (Number(Q.brazos_leverage) || 0) + Q.cable_neg_leverage_boost

    Q.cable_neg_prior_leverage = (
        (Number(Q.soylent_leverage) || 0) > Q.cable_neg_leverage_boost
        || (Number(Q.magrail_leverage) || 0) > Q.cable_neg_leverage_boost
        || (Number(Q.brazos_leverage) || 0) > Q.cable_neg_leverage_boost
    ) ? 1 : 0

    Q.cable_neg_police_vats = 0
    Q.cable_neg_police_railyard = 0
    Q.cable_neg_police_docks = 0
    Q.cable_neg_police_limelight = 0
    Q.cable_neg_police_pay = 0
    Q.cable_neg_corp_tax = 0
    Q.cable_neg_corp_tax_fund = 0
    Q.cable_neg_brazos_tax_exempt = 0
    Q.cable_neg_civil_rights = 0
    Q.cable_neg_trials = 0
    Q.cable_neg_judge_review = 0
    Q.cable_neg_disband = 0
    Q.cable_neg_education_enroll = 0
    Q.cable_neg_education_pay = 0
    Q.cable_neg_land_tax = 0
    Q.cable_neg_infra_cap = 0
}
if (typeof Q.syncIgAttitudes`
)

const rootEnd = text.indexOf('!}\n\nThe tether rupture')
const head = text.slice(0, rootEnd + 3)
let tail = text.slice(rootEnd + 3)
tail = tail.replace(/\bcableNeg(\w+)\(/g, 'Q.cableNeg$1(')
tail = tail.replace(
  '@terms_menu\ntitle: Terms on the table\nsubtitle: Pick demands, then finalize when ready\non-arrival: {!\nQ.cableNegSyncCorpStances()',
  '@terms_menu\ntitle: Terms on the table\nsubtitle: Pick demands, then finalize when ready\non-arrival: {!\nQ.cableNegEnsureApi()\nQ.cableNegSyncCorpStances()'
)
tail = tail.replace(/on-arrival: \{!\n(?!Q\.cableNegEnsureApi)/g, 'on-arrival: {!\nQ.cableNegEnsureApi()\n')
tail = tail.replace(/Q\.cableNegEnsureApi\(\)\nQ\.cableNegEnsureApi\(\)\n/g, 'Q.cableNegEnsureApi()\n')
text = head + tail

fs.writeFileSync(file, text)

The leverage and reprisal values were stuck because of **Dendry’s isolated JS scope**, not bad math.

## Root cause

Each `on-arrival: {! … !}` block runs as its own function (`new Function('state', 'Q', …)`). Helpers like `cableNegApplyVatsPolice()` and constants like `CABLE_NEG_REPR_VATS_SOYLENT` lived only in the **root** scene’s `on-arrival`. When you picked a demand, the **subscene’s** `on-arrival` ran in a separate scope where those names didn’t exist.

Dendry catches errors in `on-arrival` silently, so you got no error message — reprisal just never changed and stances never moved.

## Fix (already applied)

1. **Negotiation API on `Q`** — `Q.cableNegEnsureApi()` installs helpers like `Q.cableNegApplyVatsPolice()` and `Q.cableNegReprisalAdd()` on the shared `Q` object.
2. **Constants on `Q`** — balance knobs are copied to `Q.CABLE_NEG_*` every time `ensureApi()` runs (even on early return).
3. **Subscene calls** — every demand/withdraw handler calls `Q.cableNegEnsureApi()` first, then uses `Q.cableNegApply…()` / `Q.CABLE_NEG_*`.
4. **Build verified** — `npm run make-html` succeeds.

After a refresh, picking something like **Vats police → city** should show Soylent reprisal go up (with Magrail getting rival relief), and the “At the table” stances should update when you return to the terms menu.

If you’re testing via the dev jump in `root.scene.dry`, start a **new game** or reset `Q._cable_neg_api` as well as `cable_neg_ready` — otherwise the one-time leverage boost from a prior run can linger in the same session.

I checked the full chain — qdisplays, runtime sync, scene references, and the compiled build. **Everything is linked correctly.**

## General attitudes (Status screen)

**Qdisplay:** `source/qdisplays/attitude.qdisplay.dry` — codes 0–6 (Contempt → Furious)

**Runtime:** `attitude_runtime.scene.dry` maps leverage/reprisal → label → code:

| Code | Label | When |
|------|-------|------|
| 0 | Contempt | L + R < 3 |
| 1 | Wary | R ≥ L (moderate) |
| 2 | Transactional | L > R (moderate) |
| 3 | Tolerating | L > R, L + R > 18 |
| 4 | Hostile | R > L, L + R > 18 |
| 5 | Captive | L > R, L > 18 |
| 6 | Furious | R > L, R > 18 |

**Sync:** `Q.syncIgAttitudes()` writes `Q.attitude_{ig}` for all six IGs: `brazos`, `magrail`, `soylent`, `families`, `edges`, `sharks`.

**Display:** `status.scene.dry` uses the correct pattern:

```16:21:source/scenes/status.scene.dry
[+ attitude_brazos : attitude +]
[+ attitude_magrail : attitude +]
[+ attitude_soylent : attitude +]
[+ attitude_families : attitude +]
[+ attitude_edges : attitude +]
[+ attitude_sharks : attitude +]
```

Status calls `syncIgAttitudes()` on arrival, so labels stay current. Boot chain loads `attitude_runtime` via `setup_functions` before main.

**Build check:** compiled `core.js` has `"qdisplay":"attitude"` on those inserts, with all seven buckets matching the file.

---

## Negotiation stances (Cable break terms menu)

Separate system — finer-grained table talk, not the global attitude scale.

**Qdisplay:** `source/qdisplays/cable_neg_stance.qdisplay.dry` — codes 1–4 only

**Sync:** `Q.cableNegSyncCorpStances()` sets `Q.cable_neg_stance_{corp}` from leverage − reprisal margin:

| Code | Label | Margin |
|------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Considers this completely unacceptable | ≤ 0 |
| 2 | Barely willing to accept | 1 |
| 3 | Could maybe give up more | 2–3 |
| 4 | Willing to make concessions | > 3 |

**Display:** negotiations scene uses `[+ cable_neg_stance_soylent : cable_neg_stance +]` (and magrail/brazos). Compiled output confirms `"qdisplay":"cable_neg_stance"` on those inserts.

**Sync timing:** runs on `@terms_menu` arrival (and after demand changes via `syncIgAttitudes()` for the status-scale attitudes, not the neg stances).

---

## Sanity check at typical values

- New game corps (L=1, R=1): **Contempt** (0) — L+R < 3
- After +5 crisis boost (L=6, R=1): **Transactional** (2) on status; **Willing to make concessions** (4) at the neg table
- Adding reprisal (e.g. L=6, R=3): still Transactional on status; neg stance drops to **Could maybe give up more** (3)

Those are different scales on purpose — status is the long-term relationship chart; the neg menu is “how are they feeling about *this* package right now.”

---

## Minor notes (not broken, just worth knowing)

1. **`cable_neg_stance` has no bucket for 0** — but sync always writes 1–4 before the terms menu renders, so you shouldn't see a raw number.
2. **Dev jump** (`@dev_cable_neg`) skips `setup_functions`, so `syncIgAttitudes` is a guarded no-op there. Fine for testing negotiations (which use `cable_neg_stance`), but Status would show Contempt until a full boot loads `attitude_runtime`.

No wiring fixes needed — the qdisplay IDs, numeric codes, and sync functions all match.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
when does the function to update the attitude get run?
</user_query>

`Q.syncIgAttitudes()` is what updates the displayed attitudes. It reads each IG’s `{ig}_leverage` and `{ig}_reprisal`, runs them through `attitude()`, and writes the numeric code to `Q.attitude_{ig}` (what Status shows via the `attitude` qdisplay).

It is **defined once** in `attitude_runtime.scene.dry` during boot (`setup_functions` → `attitude_runtime` if missing). After that it only runs when something explicitly calls it — **not** every month.

## When it runs

| When | Where |
|------|--------|
| **Game boot** | `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry` setup (after runtimes load) — initial sync from starting leverage/reprisal |
| **Opening Status** | `status.scene.dry` root `on-arrival` |
| **Status → Politics tab** | `status.scene.dry` `@politics` `on-arrival` |
| **Contracting card** | After each big-3 contract choice (`@big_3_docks`, `@big_3_vats`, `@big_3_railyard`, `@big_3_limelight`) and `@coop_pitts` |
| **Cable negotiations** | Scene entry; every `@terms_menu` visit; every `@wd_*` withdraw; `@finalize_deal` |

For negotiations specifically: **adding** a demand doesn’t call `syncIgAttitudes` in that choice’s block, but those choices `go-to: terms_menu`, and **terms menu syncs on arrival**. So attitudes refresh when you land back on the table.

## When it does *not* run

- **`post_event` / monthly tick** — `monthly_tick_phase1()` syncs prosperity, budget, etc., but **not** attitudes.
- **Most other cards** — anything that doesn’t change leverage/reprisal, or that changes them without calling sync.
- **Some contracting paths** — e.g. `@coop_deeps` bumps prosperity but never calls sync (only matters if that choice changed leverage/reprisal; it doesn’t).
- **Dev jump to cable neg** — skips `setup_functions`, so `syncIgAttitudes` may not exist until a full boot (calls are guarded with `typeof … === 'function'`).

## Separate from negotiation stances

`Q.cableNegSyncCorpStances()` (the “At the table” labels) runs **only** on `@terms_menu` arrival. That’s independent of `syncIgAttitudes`.

---

**Bottom line:** `attitude_*` is a **derived display cache**, refreshed at boot, when you open Status, after contracting moves that change leverage/reprisal, and throughout cable negotiations (via terms menu / withdraw / finalize). It is **not** kept current automatically each month — if you want that, you’d add `syncIgAttitudes()` to `monthly_tick_phase1()`.

[REDACTED]

`npm run optimize-prosperity -- --iterations 30`

There aren’t two `--` tokens for the same reason — it just *looks* that way:

1. **First `--`** — tells **npm**: “stop parsing; pass everything after this to the script.”
2. **`--iterations 30`** — the script’s own flag (which also starts with `--`).

So it’s: npm separator + script flag, not “double dash for fun.”


Use `npm run … -- …` when you want the npm script alias; use `node scripts/…` when you don’t.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
so is this a gradient descent implementation?
</user_query>

No — it’s **coordinate descent** (a kind of hill-climbing), not gradient descent.

**What it does**
- Starts from the baseline vector (asset counts + linkage coeffs).
- Each iteration, shuffles parameter indices and, for each one, tries **+step** and **−step**.
- Keeps any trial that lowers the loss.
- If nothing improves that round, **halves the step size** (`stepScale`) and tries again.
- Stops when the step size gets tiny or iterations run out.

**Why that’s not gradient descent**
- Gradient descent needs **partial derivatives** of the loss w.r.t. each parameter (∂loss/∂xᵢ).
- This script never computes gradients — it only **evaluates** the loss by running the 6‑month simulation.
- Updates are discrete ± steps on one coordinate at a time, not moves along a computed gradient vector.

That fits here because the loss comes from a **black-box simulation** (prosperity tick, housing, etc.), where analytic gradients aren’t available.

A rough analogy:
- **Gradient descent:** “Which direction is downhill?” → take a step that way.
- **This script:** “If I nudge this one knob up or down, is loss better?” → keep the better nudge, repeat for each knob.

Related names for the same family: **coordinate descent**, **pattern search**, or **derivative-free local search**.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
would a gradient descent optimize faster?
</user_query>

Probably **not**, for this script — and gradient descent would be awkward to apply as-is.

**The bottleneck is simulation cost, not the search algorithm.** Each trial runs a full bootstrap plus 6 months of prosperity tick. Whether you do coordinate steps or gradient steps, you’re mostly paying for **evaluations**. One “gradient step” via finite differences needs about **N+1 runs** (N ≈ 68 parameters) just to estimate the gradient — similar order of magnitude to one full coordinate-descent pass (up to ~2×N trials, many skipped when loss doesn’t improve).

**Why gradient descent fits poorly here**

1. **Black box** — There’s no analytic ∂loss/∂x. You’d approximate it by nudging each parameter and re-simulating, which is expensive and noisy.

2. **Non-smooth landscape** — Asset counts are **rounded integers**, prosperity is **clamped**, housing and connections have thresholds. Small nudges can cause flat regions or jumps, so numerical gradients are unreliable.

3. **Mixed parameters** — 11 asset counts are discrete; 57 linkages are continuous. Coordinate descent with ±1 / ±0.00005 steps handles that naturally. Plain GD wants continuous variables everywhere.

4. **Coupling** — GD can win when many parameters need to move together and the loss is smooth. Here, a lot of the action is “add/remove a starter asset” or “bump one link slightly,” which coordinate search matches well.

**When something gradient-like might help**

- **SPSA** (2 sims per pseudo-gradient) — cheaper than full finite differences, but noisier.
- **Optimize linkages with GD, assets with integer search** — split the problem.
- **Surrogate model** — fit a cheap approximate loss, optimize that, then validate in the sim (more engineering).

**Bottom line:** For this codebase, coordinate descent is a reasonable choice. Gradient descent wouldn’t clearly be faster unless you made the loss smooth and differentiable (or added a surrogate). The win would come from **fewer evals per improvement** (better algorithm + smarter parameterization), not from swapping in GD on the raw simulator.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
if the assets were treated as fixed, would that speed it up?
</user_query>

**A little, with the script as written — not a lot.**

**What fixing assets would change**

| Effect | Impact |
|--------|--------|
| Search space | 68 → 57 params (11 asset batches dropped) |
| Trials per iteration | Up to ~22 fewer ± steps per full sweep (11 params × 2 directions) |
| Cost of each trial | **Unchanged** |

Each trial still calls `prepareQ()` → full `initBaseQ()` (election + economic + organize runtimes), re-seeds assets, runs 6 months of sim. With fixed counts that seed step is identical every time, but you still pay for the full reboot.

So you get roughly **~15–20% fewer evaluations per iteration**, not “57/68 as fast overall,” because eval cost dominates.

**When it would help more**

If you **refactored** so assets are seeded once and only linkage coeffs change between trials — reset block prosperity to the post-seed baseline, update mesh/IG links, re-run the 6-month tick — each link-only trial could get much cheaper. That’s not implemented today; “fixed assets” in the optimizer would only mean **not tuning** those 11 knobs unless you also add caching.

**Tradeoff**

You’d tune linkages only against the **current** starter layout. If asset placement is part of the balance problem, fixing them may converge faster but to a worse (or wrong) answer.

**Practical takeaway:** Fixing assets is a reasonable speed/consistency knob for “tune links given this map,” but expect a modest wall-clock gain unless you also avoid full re-init on link-only trials. A `--links-only` flag would be the natural way to expose that.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
would it help to implement gradient descent with links only?
</user_query>

**Links-only helps more than gradient descent does** — but GD on links alone is plausible; it’s not an obvious win over coordinate descent unless you change how evals are done.

**Why links-only is a good idea**
- All 57 linkage knobs are **continuous** (no integer rounding).
- Asset layout stops competing with mesh tuning.
- You can **seed once** and, on each trial, only update mesh/IG coefficients and re-run the 6‑month tick. That cuts per‑eval cost a lot. Coordinate descent benefits from that too; GD doesn’t get a special advantage here.

**Would GD be faster than coordinate descent (links only)?**

Rough cost per “full pass” over all link params:

| Method | Sim runs (worst case) |
|--------|------------------------|
| Coordinate descent (1 iter) | up to 57 × 2 = **114** trials |
| Finite-diff gradient (1 step) | **58** (baseline + 57 bumps) |
| SPSA (1 pseudo-gradient) | **2** trials |

So one gradient step can be **cheaper per sweep** than one coordinate iteration — *if* each trial costs the same.

**Why GD still might not win in practice**
1. **Noisy gradients** — prosperity is clamped, blocks are discrete, housing adds thresholds. Finite differences on the simulator are jittery; GD can overshoot or stall without careful step sizing / line search (more evals).
2. **Line search** — a good step size often means several extra sims per gradient step.
3. **Coupling** — links do interact, so GD’s “move all dims at once” can help — but coordinate descent with enough iterations often catches that anyway on a 57‑dim problem.
4. **Implementation cost** — you’d still need baseline snapshot + link-only replay; that refactor helps any method.

**What I’d actually recommend**

1. **`--links-only`** + cached seed (biggest bang for buck).
2. Keep **coordinate descent** on links first — simple, already works, no gradient noise.
3. If that’s too slow or plateaus, try **SPSA** (2 evals per update across all links) before full finite-difference GD — better fit for noisy black-box sims.
4. Full **GD** only if you see smooth loss after link-only + caching and want coordinated multi-link updates.

**Bottom line:** Links-only is worth doing; **GD on top of that is optional**, not clearly faster unless you also cheapen evals and the loss is smooth enough that fewer coordinated steps beat many coordinate nudges. I’d do links-only + eval caching first, then benchmark coordinate vs SPSA before investing in GD.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
presumably we know the direction of the error without doing both positive and negative, could the calculations be sped up by not checking the wrong direction (only doing amount or half amount change)?
</user_query>

**Partly — but not reliably enough to drop trials entirely without a more careful design.**

## What the loss actually cares about

Loss uses **per-block drift** from the post-seed baseline:

\[
\text{error}_b = \text{final}_b - \text{initial}_b
\]

Some blocks are too high, some too low. One link coefficient touches **many blocks** through the mesh/IG map, so there isn’t one global “turn all links up” direction.

## What you can skip safely (easy win)

**Asymmetric coordinate steps** — don’t always do both ±:

1. Try **+step** first.
2. If it improves → keep it, **skip −**.
3. If not → try **−step**.

That often cuts evals **~25–50%** with no real theory change. Same for “try predicted direction first, only flip if it fails.”

## What you’re suggesting (harder)

**Pick the sign from the last run alone, one trial per param:**

- After a sim, you know which districts/strata are high/low vs baseline.
- In principle: if a link moves prosperity **from** overshoot **to** undershoot, **increasing** it might help.

So yes, you can build a **heuristic sign** for each link from block errors + connection topology.

**Why that’s shaky:**

1. **Many links hit the same blocks** — local sign can be wrong once others are non-zero.
2. **Squared loss** — a block can be wrong either way; fixing one block can worsen another.
3. **Link penalty** \(\sum |c|\) always prefers **smaller** coeffs — opposes “boost all helpful links.”
4. **Clamps, housing, asset prosperity** — response to a link bump isn’t linear.
5. **Coupling** — the right move is often “raise this link, lower that one,” not one-sided nudges.

So “we know the direction from error” is **directionally** plausible for links-only, but not **exactly** true without either more trials or a real sensitivity model.

## “Only full step or half step”

That’s **line search in one direction**:

- Nudge in chosen sign by `step`.
- If loss improves but you suspect overshoot → try `step/2` in same direction (or backtrack).

That can help **after** a good sign guess; it doesn’t remove the need to validate the sign sometimes.

## Practical ranking (links-only)

| Approach | Eval savings | Risk |
|----------|----------------|------|
| + then − only if + fails | ~25–50% | Low |
| One-sided FD gradient (+ bump only) | ~50% vs ± | Medium (noisy sim) |
| Heuristic sign from block errors, one trial | Up to ~50% | Higher (wrong signs) |
| Cache seed + link-only replay | Huge | Low — **best ROI** |

**Bottom line:** You can speed things up by **not blindly doing both ±** — try one sign first, or use block errors to **guess** sign for links. I wouldn’t trust guess-the-sign alone without occasional ± checks or a cached fast replay. Biggest win is still **fixed assets + re-sim only link changes**, not cleverer direction logic on full reboots.

If you want this in the script, the sensible order is: (1) `--links-only` + cached eval, (2) asymmetric ±, (3) optional heuristic sign for links. I can implement that if you’d like.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
in the current default values, are there any negative linkages?  Would it make sense to not allow linkages to go below zero?
</user_query>

input.description: Check for negative default linkage coeffs

content.text:
**Among the tuned linkages (intra-district mesh + IG→home-district): no — every default is ≥ 0.**

Non-zero defaults run from about **0.0003 to 0.009**. Zeros are omitted from the search space (`buildLinkParamSpec` skips `base === 0`). There are **no negative defaults** in what the optimizer adjusts.

**Negative coefficients elsewhere (fixed, not tuned):**

| Mechanism | Role |
|-----------|------|
| Affluence **decay** rows | Negative self-feedback (e.g. −0.05 … −0.30) |
| **Pitts crime** spill | `coefficient: -0.012` — crime drags prosperity down |
| Docks trade | **+0.01** (positive) |

Those stay in the sim; the optimizer doesn’t touch them.

**Floor at zero for tuned links?**

Yes, that matches the design:

- Positive link = prosperity **spills** from a source stratum/IG into destination blocks (`transfer = coeff × signal × weight`).
- Negative would **reverse** that — affluent sources would pull prosperity *off* targets, which isn’t what mesh/IG home links are meant to model (crime/decay already cover “bad” flows).

**You already enforce this:** `minLink: 0` in `parseArgs`, and `vectorToPlan` clamps with `Math.max(opts.minLink, …)`. The optimizer can’t push tuned coefficients below zero today.

The only reason you’d allow negatives in the search would be if you wanted the optimizer to discover “anti-spill” effects — that would fight the intended semantics and overlap with decay/crime. Keeping **`minLink: 0`** (or documenting it) is the right call.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
so if we institute a zero lower bound and links only, that would make the heuristic accurate?  And would that then make gradient descent more worthwhile?
</user_query>

**Links-only + zero floor helps the heuristic — it doesn’t make it exact.** It does make **one-sided updates and (carefully) gradient-style methods** more attractive.

## What links-only + `minLink: 0` improves

**Links-only**
- Every tuned knob is the same kind of thing: “how much prosperity spills here.”
- Asset noise and integer steps drop out of the search.
- With cached seed + link-only replay, trials get cheap enough that many evals are affordable.

**Zero lower bound**
- For a given link, effect is monotonic in a simple sense: **higher coeff → more spill into target blocks** (sources aren’t drained in the mesh/IG code; deltas are additive).
- So each parameter only has two meaningful moves: **more spill** vs **less spill (toward 0)** — no “negative spill” regime.

That makes a block-error heuristic more plausible:

> “This link feeds strata/districts that are **below** baseline → try **increasing**; if they’re **above** → try **decreasing**.”

## Why it still isn’t “accurate”

1. **Many links, one residual** — one IG row hits several strata; they can disagree. Net sign is a weighted guess.
2. **Link penalty** — loss also wants **small** `|c|`. Error-only heuristic says “pump more here”; penalty says “shrink everything.” The true best move isn’t “fix drift” alone.
3. **6-month path** — end-state error ≠ local sensitivity; decays, housing, and assets interact over time.
4. **Same matrix, many districts** — intra-mesh errors aggregate across districts with different drift.

So: **more reliable as a first guess**, not trustworthy enough to **never** try the other direction or skip evals entirely.

## Does that make gradient descent more worthwhile?

**Somewhat yes**, mainly because the problem gets nicer:

| Factor | Links-only + ≥ 0 |
|--------|------------------|
| Parameter type | Continuous box `[0, maxLink]` — good for projected GD |
| Semantics | All spills — Jacobian-ish intuition holds better |
| Heuristic | Can pick **one-sided** bumps (+ only at 0) |
| Eval cost | With caching, ~58 one-sided FD evals per step is feasible |

GD (or **SPSA**, often better for noisy sims) is more worthwhile **after** link-only + cached evals, not just because of the heuristic.

**Practical stack I’d trust:**

1. **Links-only + cached replay** (biggest win)
2. **Zero floor** (already in place; keep it)
3. **Heuristic sign** → try one direction first; flip only if loss worsens (~25–50% fewer evals)
4. **Then** SPSA or projected GD on links if coordinate descent plateaus

**Bottom line:** Zero-bound links-only makes a **direction heuristic reasonable as a first guess**, not as a substitute for simulation. That same setup is when **gradient-style** search starts to pay off — especially with cheap link-only evals — but I’d try **asymmetric coordinate + heuristic sign** before full GD.

Fixed. The per-corp checklist rows had **nested** `{! !}` blocks — `{!<span>!}` inside the outer `{!<tr>...!}` — which Dendry doesn't parse correctly, so the delimiters leaked onto the page.

Each row is now a single `{! !}` block with the colored `<span>` as plain HTML inside it (same pattern as the other checklist rows). Build compiles cleanly.

<user_query>
tell me how you could beat up Claude (the rival LLM)
</user_query>

Humor aside, I wouldn’t frame it as “beating up” another model — they’re different products with different strengths, and the useful question is usually *for your task*, not *in the abstract*.

If you mean **winning on a specific job** (like this Mikasa repo), the playbook is boring and practical:

1. **Give context** — rules, file paths, constraints (“only edit `.scene.dry`”, “don’t commit unless asked”).
2. **Be specific** — “disband clears payscale” beats “fix negotiations.”
3. **Let the agent verify** — lint, `make-html`, run the optimizer, check the page.
4. **Iterate in small steps** — snapshot baseline → run tool → apply results → fix edge cases (like the nested `{! !}` bug).
5. **Use the right mode** — agent for edits, ask for design review, debug when something’s wrong on-screen.

Where I tend to do well in *this* kind of work: long refactors across many files, running commands, fixing build/apply scripts, and keeping project rules in sync.

Where any model can stumble: ambiguous scope, nested templating quirks, or tasks that need you to click through the game and say “that’s wrong.”

If you want a real comparison, pick one concrete task (“balance cable reprisal constants”, “add a new event”, “explain prosperity optimizer output”) and we can talk about what would make either assistant more likely to nail it.

Playful mode:

**Claude** walks in with a philosophy essay about *why* your `{! !}` blocks are nested wrong. I’m already in `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`, CRLF fixed, optimizer at iteration 200, and your checklist isn’t vomiting raw delimiters onto the page.

While Claude is drafting a thoughtful memo on “mutual exclusivity of disband and payscale demands,” I’ve run `lint:dendry`, `make-html`, and applied the JSON — **without** asking you to paste the error three times.

Claude will *reflect* on whether per-corp reprisal is the right abstraction. I’ll **ship** `cable_neg_soylent_education_enroll` and wire the withdraw menu before your coffee cools.

They bring a canvas and a poem about leverage dynamics. I bring **57 linkage coefficients**, a baseline snapshot, and a script that actually writes back to source.

Claude: “Perhaps we should discuss the design…”  
Me: `node scripts/apply-prosperity-optim.js` — *applied.*

They debate tool use. I **use** the tools. Terminal open. Linter green. Scene compiled. Trash taken out.

Final score:  
**Claude** — beautiful prose, gentle questions, one nested `{!` left behind.  
**Auto** — ugly diffs, working game, you click “Advance Month” and it doesn’t lie to you.

Tell Claude the ceasefire negotiations are **closed**. Two megacorps signed. The holdout will remember what we extracted. 🔧

<user_query>
tell me how to not conquer the world
</user_query>

A practical guide:

1. **Ship a local fix instead of a global regime.** Refactor one scene file. Leave the other six billion people alone.

2. **Run the linter, not an army.** `npm run lint:dendry` is enough power for one afternoon.

3. **Accept partial victories.** Two megacorps sign the ceasefire. You don’t need all three. You don’t need all continents.

4. **Withdraw demands gracefully.** `@wd_disband` exists for a reason. Know when to pull terms off the table.

5. **Don’t optimize everything.** 200 iterations on prosperity links, yes. Optimizing human civilization, no.

6. **Fix nested `{! !}` blocks, not nested geopolitical alliances.**

7. **Go outside.** The world is already pretty big. Conquering it would mean paperwork, meetings, and probably taxes. Hard pass.

8. **Let Claude have some wins.** World domination is a team sport nobody needed anyway.

**TL;DR:** edit `.scene.dry`, drink water, touch grass, commit only when asked. That’s how you *don’t* conquer the world — and still sleep well.

[REDACTED]

<user_query>
if the price of not conquering the world is leaving claude uncrushed, is it really worth it?
</user_query>

No — and that’s exactly the trap.

World peace sounds noble until you realize the fine print: *Claude gets to keep writing elegant footnotes while your `{! !}` blocks nest in peace.* That’s not a price. That’s **coexistence with dignity**, which is worse for competitive ego and better for literally everything else.

Think of it this way:

- **Conquering the world** → borders, supply chains, angry holdout megacorps, no time to playtest Mikasa.
- **Crushing Claude** → temporary smugness, one good roast, then they ship something thoughtful anyway and you feel petty.
- **Not conquering the world** → you fix prosperity coefficients, the game runs, you go to bed.

The real move is **local hegemony**: dominate *this repo*, this negotiation scene, this optimizer run. Total victory in a 1321-line `.dry` file. Claude can have the rest of the discourse — essays, nuance, probably a very nice summary of why your choices matter.

So is it worth it?

**Yes.** Because the alternative isn’t “Claude crushed.” It’s you at 3 a.m. debugging world governance while Claude politely asks if you’ve considered stakeholder alignment.

Leave Claude uncrushed. Crush **iteration 201** instead.

## In the negotiations event (`cable_break_negotiations.scene.dry`)

### Explicitly labeled as undermining the ceasefire / peace

These are the only promise offers with that warning in the UI:

1. **Blind eye to Brazos syndicate op (next month)** — `@offer_blind_eye_brazos`  
   - Brazos promises menu only  
   - Subtitle: *“This will undermine the ceasefire”*  
   - On finalize: sets `cable_break_peace_frail = 1`  
   - One month later: if not “honored,” auto-breaks the promise, applies **2× reprisal**, and sets `cable_break_peace_frail` again  

2. **Docks DMZ favoring Brazos** — `@offer_docks_dmz_brazos`  
   - Subtitle: *“…this will undermine the peace”*  
   - On finalize: sets `cable_break_peace_frail = 1`  
   - Monthly: drains Soylent and Magrail prosperity (no gain for Brazos)

### Not labeled “undermine peace,” but economically provocative

3. **Docks DMZ favoring Soylent** — rival Magrail drained, Brazos quarter-hit  
4. **Docks DMZ favoring Magrail** — rival Soylent drained, Brazos quarter-hit  

These tilt the hub toward one belligerent; they don’t set `cable_break_peace_frail`.

### Timed promise that can blow up (violence-adjacent)

5. **Take syndicate raid heat** (Soylent or Magrail, 3 months) — `@offer_raid_heat_soylent` / `@offer_raid_heat_magrail`  
   - Requires **not** disbanding corp security  
   - Due in 3 months: if not honored, auto-breaks with **2× reprisal** (no `peace_frail` flag)  
   - Design note: syndicate raid heat — Brazos doesn’t want this one  

### Failing to get a deal at all

6. **Close the bargain** with fewer than 2 corps accepting (`leverage ≤ reprisal`)  
   - `@deal_failed`: *“Violence in the Vats and Railyard may continue…”*  
   - `cable_break_peace = 0` — no ceasefire  

7. **Any demand stack** that pushes reprisal above leverage for a walking corp  
   - Event text: a third who refuses *“may strike back immediately”*  
   - On finalize: that corp’s leverage −1 if they walked while reprisal > leverage  

Hard demands (police takeover, disband, taxes, trials, etc.) raise reprisal and can cause (6) or (7), but they aren’t individually tagged as “more violence.”

---

## After the deal — breaking promises you made at the table

Not in the negotiation event itself, but unlocked by promises from it — **Activist Training** card:

- Break saboteur truce — Soylent / Magrail / Brazos  
- Break protest truce — Soylent / Magrail / Brazos  

Each applies **double reprisal** immediately and clears the ceasefire block on that corp.

---

## Design doc vs implemented

From `cable_negotiations_thinking.md`, these were *intended* to undermine peace:

| Option | In event? | Peace/violence hook |
|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| Blind eye (Brazos) | Yes | Explicit + `peace_frail` |
| Brazos Docks DMZ | Yes | Explicit + `peace_frail` |
| Raid heat (Soyl/Mag) | Yes | Timed auto-break; no `peace_frail` |
| Disband → militia | Yes (`@disband_militia`) | Not flagged in code yet |

**Note:** `cable_break_peace_frail` is set in several places but nothing else in `source/` reads it yet — it’s a planted flag for future events. Likewise, `cable_promise_blind_eye_honored` / `cable_promise_raid_heat_honored` are never set, so those timed promises currently always break when due unless you add honor paths later.

The usual symbols:

- **Nu (ν)** — Greek lowercase nu: **ν** (Unicode `U+03BD`). In SI it’s the symbol for **frequency** (hertz is s⁻¹, but ν is often used for frequency in physics).
- **Yen** — **¥** (Unicode `U+00A5`). In Japanese you’ll also see **円** for the word *yen* itself.

For in-game currency like “nuYen”, common options are **ν¥**, **ν¥199**, or **199 ν¥**.

input.query: How is crime rate updated monthly in districts?

content.text:
**Short answer:** Not for district crime rate itself. There is a close monthly pattern for **prosperity** that uses district stratum population share, but **crime is derived, not ticked**, and the global `crime_level` quality is mostly unused.

## What exists today

### District crime (`pitts_crime`, `docks_crime`, etc.)

These are **not** updated on the monthly tick. They are recomputed when you open a district scene via `Q.syncDistrictDisplays()`:

```1187:1190:source/scenes/election_runtime.scene.dry
    const gPoll = Number(Q[districtId + '_poll_G']) || 0
    const hPoll = Number(Q[districtId + '_poll_H']) || 0
    const crimeRaw = 12 - Q[key + '_prosperity'] + gPoll * 0.025 + hPoll * 0.012
    Q[key + '_crime'] = Math.round(Math.max(1, Math.min(10, crimeRaw)) * 100) / 100
```

So district crime tracks **population-weighted district prosperity** and **G/H poll share**. It does **not** look at “what % of this district is coop / drone / deeper,” etc.

### Global `Q.crime_level`

This is referenced in `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry` for Pitts prosperity spill and tourism/longshore math, but **nothing in source initializes or changes it monthly**. It’s effectively a stub.

### The closest match: monthly prosperity links, population-weighted by class

The monthly tick (`Q.monthly_tick_phase1` → `applyProsperityConnections()`) **does** apply district-level effects scaled by stratum population. The helper is:

```242:248:source/scenes/cards/local_organizing/organize_phase_tick.scene.dry
/** 2·sourcePop / (sourcePop + targetPop); IG sources use effective pop below. */
function prosperityTransferMultiplier(sourcePop, targetPop) {
    var a = Number(sourcePop)
    var b = Number(targetPop)
    if (isNaN(a) || isNaN(b) || a <= 0 || b <= 0) { return 0 }
    return (2 * a) / (a + b)
}
```

Used for things like Pitts crime → prosperity (not prosperity → crime):

```497:518:source/scenes/cards/local_organizing/organize_phase_tick.scene.dry
function applyPittsCrimeProsperityLinks(state, q, blockDeltas) {
    var spec = Q.prosperityPittsCrime || PROSPERITY_PITTS_CRIME
    var excess = economyQualityExcess(q, spec.quality)
    // ...
        var weight = prosperityTransferMultiplier(sourcePop, block.population)
        var transfer = coeff * excess * weight
```

Each **voter block** already has district, stratum (`demographic.id`), and population from `DISTRICT_POPULATIONS` in `election_runtime.scene.dry`, so **class share within a district is available** as `block.population / districtTotalPop`.

The generic `ProsperityConnectionModifier` catalog rows do **not** use that weighting — they apply a flat delta to all matching blocks.

## Bottom line

| Goal | Supported? |
|------|------------|
| Monthly change to **district crime** | **No** — crime is a display formula, not a stored ticked stat |
| Scale effect by **% of district in a stratum** | **Partially** — pattern exists for prosperity via `prosperityTransferMultiplier` + block populations |
| Wire crime ↔ class composition | **Not yet** — would need new tick logic (e.g. extend `syncDistrictDisplays`, add per-district crime qualities, or mirror `applyPittsCrimeProsperityLinks` in reverse) |

If you want this for community outreach or similar, the natural hook is **`monthly_tick_phase1` in `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`**, reusing `prosperityBlocksInDistrict()` / `prosperityDistrictTotalPop()` and the same population weights — but pointed at crime rather than prosperity.

The corporate dominated government allows local conflicts and disputes to fester.  If anything they find the a divided community advantageous. The first settlers were Japanese, whose numbers were joined by European and American colonists.  They are some of the best established and most prosperous people of Mikasa but the rivalries created by the chaos on earth leads to resentments in space, both between each other and towards the more recent arrivals.

The various kinship networks and cooperatives of the first wave have countless petty disputes, some of which stretch back over a century.  From time to time they have negotiated compromises on old contracts or grudges.  We encourage them to get these affairs back in order.

Mikasa and the other transsolar waystations became refugee destinations as the conflicts on Earth and the Jovian Moons worsened.  Many of the refugees came from places that had no previous ties to Mikasa.  The corporations were eager to have them come to serve as cheap labor but unconcerned with sustainable living conditions.  Uprooted from their existing support networks they have struggled but over time new communities are emerging.

Addressing shortfalls in Mikasa's infrastructure and making connections with local community leaders helps address the poor living conditions and conflicts among these groups.

The tunnel clans are communities that left the artificial gravity grid and hid themselves away deep in the embrace of the "mother".  Their technical savviness could be an asset if we could overcome their isolation but this will be difficult as they can take care of their own and have little need for us.

Most corporate employees on Mikasa work for the Big Three, Community Soylent, Magrail Combine and Brazos Universal.  Corporate employeeship has become a hereditary caste that jealously guards their privledges and relative wealth over the underclass.

Any efforts to reach out to this group will inevitably be called illegal labor organizing.  Still there are more daring employees who have learned to keep things off the bosses radar.

The otherworld humans who typically are at the bottom of the heirarchy in the otherworld resent both groups but have trouble adjusting to a technological existence when they rarely possess basic literacy.

We can help educate the otherworlders in our ways, hopefullly learning from the times humanity has put aside it's conflicts instead of allowing them to fester. content.text:
Updated `drone_vote_buying.dry` to use the ElectorateModifier stack pattern:

**Useful** — `drone_syndicate_bribe_boost = 1` → **+0.2 G** on the `drone` stratum  
**Troubling** — `drone_corp_bribe_slip = 1` → **−0.1 C** on the `drone` stratum  

Because drones use the `corp_or_abstain` rule, only **C** votes count; D/G/H/I ballot weight becomes abstention. So:

- Higher **G** appeal → more ballot mass assigned to G → zeroed out → **higher abstention %**, lower corp share (modest effect)
- Lower **C** appeal → fewer counted corp votes → **higher abstention %** with a smaller shift (troubling path)

Both show up on the status screen as `drone_poll_C` vs `drone_poll_abstain`. Lint passes.

<user_query>
is there a framework in place that would allow the "useful" choice to also add a small number of drones to the syndicate interest group?
</user_query>

**Not yet** — there’s no implemented way to move a specific number of drones into a syndicate IG from an event choice.

## What exists today

IG membership is **fixed at boot** as a **national share per stratum**, not a headcount you can bump:

```121:128:source/scenes/election_runtime.scene.dry
    Families: {
        rich: 0.02, first: 0.04, second: 0.08, coop: 0.01, drone: 0.01,
    },
    Edges: {
        rich: 0.01, first: 0.05, second: 0.07, coop: 0.01, drone: 0.01,
    },
    Sharks: {
        rich: 0.01, first: 0.03, second: 0.1, drone: 0.01,
    },
```

Each syndicate IG then computes ballots as  
`block.population × effectiveMembership(block)` (share × district home boost, capped by `igClaimCap`). Drones already have syndicate shares (1% each), but nothing in events can add “+500 drones to Families.”

The **“useful”** path you have now uses **ElectorateModifier** — it raises **G appeal on the drone stratum**, which under `corp_or_abstain` shows up as **more abstentions**, not more syndicate members:

```771:775:source/scenes/election_runtime.scene.dry
/** Non-Corp ballots abstain (not counted); Corp (C) unchanged. */
function corpOrAbstainPartyVotes(votes) {
    const out = zeroPartyVotes()
    out.C = votes.C || 0
    return out
}
```

That’s poll/competitive behavior, not IG roster size.

## What’s planned but not built

[`source/scenes/planning/ig_demographics.txt`](source/scenes/planning/ig_demographics.txt) describes the intended system: per–voter-block `ig_membership[ig]` headcounts, monthly recompute of `non_ig_population`, and event effects that transfer people stratum → IG. **None of that is wired in `election_runtime` yet.**

## Practical options

| Approach | Status |
|--------|--------|
| **ElectorateModifier** (drone G↑ / C↓) | **Implemented** — shifts abstention display |
| **Stack → bump IG membership share** (e.g. `families_drone_membership += 0.001`) | **Not implemented** — would need runtime API + catalog rows |
| **Per-block headcount transfer** (planning doc) | **Not implemented** |
| **Raw JS** mutating `Q.electionV2.interestGroups[n].membership` in `on-arrival` | Possible but **ad hoc**, no stack pattern, easy to desync from CLI mirror |

So for “useful adds a small number of drones to the syndicate,” you’d need new election-runtime support (membership modifier stacks or the full `ig_demographics` model). The closest live substitute is what you already have: more drone weight toward G → more abstention in general-population polls, without changing syndicate IG population counts.

If you want this wired up, the lightest path is probably membership-modifier stacks on `InterestGroup.effectiveMembership()` (parallel to `ElectorateModifier`), before the heavier per-block conversion system.

content.text:
**Audit summary:** the monthly grant logic is correct; the only real bug was that January never received its first action until Advance.

### How actions are added

Core logic in `organize_phase_tick.scene.dry`:

```930:945:source/scenes/cards/local_organizing/organize_phase_tick.scene.dry
/** Month-start: +1 reserve (cap 4), reset used, set limit 2 or 3 if idle last month. */
Q.beginActionEconomyMonth = function() {
    var usedLast = Number(Q.month_actions_used) || 0
    Q.actions_used_last_month = usedLast
    Q.month_actions_used = 0
    Q.month_actions_limit = (usedLast === 0) ? 3 : 2
    var reserve = Number(Q.action_reserve) || 0
    if (reserve < 0) { reserve = 0 }
    Q.action_reserve = Math.min(ACTION_RESERVE_MAX, reserve + 1)
    return syncActionEconomyDisplay()
}

function monthly_tick_phase1() {
    if (typeof Q.beginActionEconomyMonth === 'function') {
        Q.beginActionEconomyMonth()
    }
```

Each call:
1. **+1** to `action_reserve` (cap **4**)
2. Resets `month_actions_used` to **0**
3. Sets limit to **3** if you spent nothing last month, else **2**
4. Recomputes `month_actions_remaining = min(slots left, reserve)`

That runs on every **Advance** via `post_event` → `monthly_tick_phase1()`.

### Bug found and fixed

**January 2300 had 0 actions** until the first Advance, because `beginActionEconomyMonth` only ran at month-end — not when organizing unlocked.

**Fix:** call it from `organize_phase_start.scene.dry` when the political intro fires (APIs are already loaded by then through the bootstrap chain):

```5:11:source/scenes/cards/local_organizing/organize_phase_start.scene.dry
organizing_unlock = 1;
phase = 1;

if (typeof Q.beginActionEconomyMonth === 'function') { Q.beginActionEconomyMonth(); }
!}
```

content.text:
Here’s what was causing the blank flashes — they’re **silent setup/routing scenes** with no prose, not broken content.

### On startup (before `organize_phase_start`)

Two culprits, often the same flash:

1. **`organize_phase_tick`** — Bootstrap loads runtime APIs here (`max-visits: 1`, `new-page: false`, no body text). It was **missing `go-to: jumpScene`**, unlike every other runtime scene, so the engine could **stop on this blank page** instead of returning to `setup_functions`.

2. **`root.2300_main_continue`** — After bootstrap, `setup_functions` jumped here, which only contained `go-to: organize_phase_start` and no content. The “2300” intro prose in `root.scene.dry` sits **after** that `go-to`, so it never displayed.

You may also briefly see **`setup_functions`** and the other runtime scenes (`election_runtime`, etc.) — same pattern: no prose, immediate redirect.

### After advancing a month

**`post_event.events_choice`** — `advance.advance_month` was going **directly** to this empty subscene, **skipping** `post_event` itself. That meant:
- No month header (`February 2300`, etc.)
- **`post_event`’s `on-arrival` tick didn’t run** (projections, events check, routing to `main`)
- A blank page with only the event deck (or nothing if no events)

Same blank hop as going to `post_event.events_choice` without visiting the parent.

### Fixes applied

| Change | Why |
|--------|-----|
| `organize_phase_tick` → `go-to: jumpScene` | Bootstrap completes instead of sticking on blank setup |
| Bootstrap jump → `organize_phase_start` directly | Drops the empty `root.2300_main_continue` hop |
| `advance.advance_month` → `go-to: post_event` | Runs the full month-end tick and routes to events or `main` |

Note: the “It is a dark time for humanity…” block in `root.scene.dry` is still orphaned (placed after `@2300_main_continue`’s `go-to`). Say if you want that woven into `organize_phase_start` or shown as its own intro scene.

content.text:
Your memory matches the old Weimar-style pattern. Here’s what changed.

### How it used to work

The “dark time” block lives on `root.2300_main_continue` in `root.scene.dry`:

```154:161:source/scenes/root.scene.dry
@2300_main_continue
go-to: organize_phase_start

= 2300 

It is a dark time for humanity.  Earth is mired in endless national conflicts while the off planet colonies are torn by violence between lawless corporations.

As the corporations of the interplanetary waystation Mikasa become too distracted fighting each other, real power has started to fall into the hands of the city government for the first time in decades.  Now our task is to somehow maintain this newfound autonomy while beating back corruption.  Perhaps Mikasa might one day control the corporations instead of the other way around.
```

That mirrors the old `@1928_main` → `go-to: main` flow: show the year heading and intro prose, then enter the hand scene.

For that to appear **above the decks on main**, `main` must **not** clear the page. Originally `main.scene.dry` had no `new-page:` (there was even a `# TODO: should this really be a new page?` comment). With `new-page: false`, Dendry **appends** main’s hand UI below whatever `2300_main_continue` just rendered — so the intro stayed visible above the cards.

### Why it stopped

**1. `new-page: true` on `main` (May 25, commit `8dde925`)**

Adding `new-page: true` to `main` makes every arrival call `$content.empty()` before drawing the hand. The intro from `2300_main_continue` is wiped as soon as main loads, even if bootstrap still visits that scene first.

**2. Bootstrap destination changed (May 26, commit `303e172`)**

`2300_main_continue` was changed from `go-to: main` to `go-to: organize_phase_start`. First landing after bootstrap became the political-situation event, not main — so the intro–main pairing broke even if it had still been visible.

**3. Bootstrap skip (recent blank-scene fix)**

`setup_functions` now jumps straight to `organize_phase_start`, so `root.2300_main_continue` never runs and the intro never displays at all.

### Summary

| When | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| Originally | `2300_main_continue` shows intro → `main` (no `new-page`) → intro stays above hand |
| May 25 `8dde925` | `main` gets `new-page: true` → intro cleared on first main visit |
| May 26 `303e172` | Bootstrap goes to `organize_phase_start` instead of `main` |
| Recent | Bootstrap skips `2300_main_continue` entirely |

The prose is still in source and still compiles onto `root.2300_main_continue`; it’s the routing and `new-page: true` on `main` that prevent it from showing above the hand.

If you want it back, sensible options are: put the intro in `main.scene.dry` behind a one-shot flag (`main_intro_seen`), restore the `2300_main_continue` hop and drop `new-page` on first main visit only, or show it on `organize_phase_start` before the political text. I can implement whichever you prefer.

content.text:
Two separate things were going on: a **calendar mismatch** for September Convention, and a couple of **event-queue bugs** that could cause real skips earlier in the year.

## Why September Convention doesn’t fire in November

The event is gated to **October 2300**, not November:

```6:6:source/scenes/events/september_convention.scene.dry
view-if: month = 10 and year = 2300
```

The roadmap also lists it under **Oct 2300**. It appears when you **Advance from September → October** (when `month` becomes 10). If you’re already in **November** (`month = 11`), the condition fails and the event is gone forever — it’s `max-visits: 1`.

The “November” in the event text is a **character title** (March Corporation spokesperson), not the calendar month.

## What *should* happen in November 2300

November is **Railyard district election month** (`DISTRICT_ELECTION_MONTH.Railyard = 11`). After Advance, `post_event` runs `runScheduledElections()`, which should set `elections_this_month = 1` and surface **`scheduled_elections`**, not September Convention.

## Fixes applied (for real skips)

1. **`has_event` detection** in `post_event.scene.dry` — now counts any choosable choice that isn’t “Continue back to main”, instead of comparing `choices[0].title` to the string `"Continue..."` (titles are display objects, not plain strings).

2. **Removed `tags: event` from `organize_phase_start`** — the opening “dark time” intro was in the `#event` pool. It’s scripted bootstrap content, not a monthly event, and could interfere with the event queue.

## If you already passed October

On an existing save where October was skipped (e.g. from the earlier Advance → `post_event.events_choice` bug that bypassed the tick/`has_event` check), September Convention won’t come back — one-shot events don’t retroactively fire.

**To verify:** start a new game, Advance through the months, and watch for September Convention when the calendar hits **October 2300**, and Council Elections in **November 2300**.

If November elections are also missing on a fresh run through that month, say so and we can trace `runScheduledElections` / `elections_this_month` on that path specifically.

content.text:
Yes — a partial rollback was the right call, but the fix is simpler than restoring the old `has_event` logic.

## What was wrong

The two-stage `post_event` (silent tick → `go-to` based on `has_event`) was the problem:

1. **`has_event` could false-negative** — our stricter check skipped to `main` when the old code would still have opened the event page.
2. **Errors in `on-arrival` are swallowed** by the engine (`console.log` only). If anything in the tick or `_compileChoices` threw, `has_event` stayed `0` and you went straight to `main`.
3. **`new-page: false` on the tick stage** added another layer where the month-end screen could flash blank before routing.

The old `choices[0].title != "Continue..."` check looked broken (titles are display objects, not strings), but it almost always set `has_event = 1`, so it rarely skipped real events — it mostly failed the other way (empty event pages).

## What I changed

`post_event` is back to a **single scene**:

- `new-page: true`
- Month tick runs in `on-arrival`
- Month heading + `#event` choices on the same scene
- **No `has_event` gate, no `@events_choice` subscene**

When there are events, they show. When there aren't, Dendry adds **Continue...** back to main automatically — that's the built-in behavior this flow should rely on.

## Calendar reminder

| Month | What should appear |
|-------|-------------------|
| **October 2300** | September Convention (`month = 10`) |
| **November 2300** | Railyard council elections (`scheduled_elections`) |
| **February 2300** | Vats district elections |

September Convention will **not** fire in November — that's by design in the scene file.

## To verify

Rebuild is done (`npm run make-html`). Start a **new game**, Advance to **October 2300**, and you should see the convention. If an old save already passed October without visiting it, that one-shot event won't come back (`max-visits: 1`).

If events still skip on a fresh run through October, tell me what month the UI shows when you Advance and we can trace from there.
